text: 1,2 2,7 , Bolun Li3, Benjamin Dechant 4,5, Mingzhu Xu2, 6, Sai Qu6, Guofang Miao 2, Jiye Leng7, Rong Shang 2, 10, Youngryel Ryu 11 & Photosynthetic efficiency (PE) quantifies the fraction of absorbed light used in photochemistry to produce chemical energy during photosynthesis and is essential for understanding ecosystem productivity and the global carbon cycle, particularly under conditions of vegetation stress. However, nearly 60% of the global spatiotemporal variance in terrestrial PE remains unexplained. Here we integrate remote sensing and eco-evolutionary optimality theory to derive key plant traits, alongside explainable machine learning and global eddy covariance observations, to uncover the drivers of daily PE variations. Incorporating plant traits into our model increases the explained daily PE variance from 36% to 80% for C3 vegetation and from 54% to 84% for C4 vegetation compared with using climate data alone. Key plant traits—including chlorophyll content, leaf longevity and leaf mass per area— consistently emerge as important factors across global biomes and temporal scales. Water availability and light conditions are also critical in regulating PE, underscoring the need for an integrative approach that combines plant traits with climatic factors. Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of remote sensing and eco-evolutionary optimality theory to capture principal PE drivers, offering valuable tools for more accurately predicting ecosystem Plant photosynthesis is the fundamental process that sustains ecosystem function, drives the carbon cycle, regulates atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) levels and influences global climate dynamics1,2.

text: Photosynthetic efficiency (PE) or light use efficiency, defined as the ratio of gross primary productivity (GPP) to absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (APAR), is a crucial metric for assessing how effectively ecosystems use the energy from absorbed sunlight for photosynthesis3. Understanding and optimizing PE is essential for improving crop yields, enhancing productivity and improving Earth system models under climate change. carbon sequestration and developing sustainable strategies to mitigate climate change4–8. However, around 60% of the spatiotemporal variability in ecosystem-scale PE remains unexplained9,10, underscoring the urgent need to better understand the factors that control this essential process. Integrating plant traits offers a promising path to advancing our knowledge of ecosystem PE. title: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency

text: 924 physiological mechanisms9,10,13–20, they collectively explain less than half of the spatiotemporal variation in ecosystem-scale PE9,10. In contrast, plant traits—including morphological, anatomical and biochemical features—mechanistically determine how plants respond to environmental cues and regulate photosynthetic machinery21–24. For example, leaf chlorophyll content (Chl) and the maximum carboxylation rate (Vcmax) of Rubisco are central to photosynthesis due to their direct roles in light absorption and the Calvin–Benson cycle, which assimilates CO2 into carbohydrate2,15,25. Additionally, leaf longevity (LL) is one fundamental trait in the leaf economic spectrum that can serve as an indicator of other photosynthetic traits22,26. LL and leaf mass per area (LMA) reflect plants’ strategies to optimize carbon gain relative to structural investment26–29. Canopy structure, including leaf area index (LAI) and clumping index (CIclump), directly impacts light absorption through radiative transfer30. Despite their importance, these traits remain underexplored for estimating ecosystem-scale PE. Linking plant traits to macroscale PE remains challenging due to the scarcity of spatiotemporally synchronized trait data and the difficulty of upscaling in situ measurements to align with eddy covariance flux observations31,32. Although efforts have been made to link plant traits with GPP31,33–35, debate persists about their effectiveness in predicting ecosystem functional properties36–38, which serve as unified metrics that describe ecosystem processes and responses in a comparable way, such as PE4,5. This raises several critical questions4: To what extent do plant traits capture the substantial unexplained (60%) variability of ecosystem PE across global biomes? How do canopy structure and climatic conditions influence the relationship between plant traits and ecosystem PE?

text: Here we integrate remote sensing (RS) and eco-evolutionary optimality (EEO) theory to address the challenge of unavailable in situ plant trait measurements at eddy covariance towers. EEO theory hypothesizes that plant traits evolve to optimize characteristics that balance competing needs, making them the best fit for their environment26. By leveraging data from the global eddy covariance network (120 sites, FLUXNET2015), we aim to understand the contributions of plant traits and climate to the variance in daily ecosystem PE during the growing season across various terrestrial ecosystems. Using explainable machine learning methods, we seek to elucidate the mechanisms driving ecosystem-scale PE in the terrestrial biosphere.
section: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency
title: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency

text: To quantify the extent to which plant traits contribute to the variation in ecosystem PE across global biomes, we employed three scenarios: climatic factors only, plant traits only and a combination of all factors. Our results show that climatic factors alone account for merely 36% of the spatiotemporal variance in daily PE (Fig. 1a,d), consistent with current understanding of environmental controls9,10. In contrast, plant traits alone explain a substantial 67% of the variance (Fig. 1b,e), with static (growing season mean) plant traits contributing 36% (Extended Data Fig. 1). Although EEO-based traits reflect long-term climate acclimations, explicitly integrating them into models markedly enhances predictive performance, as machine learning models alone cannot fully capture these climate-driven transformations. By incorporating both daily climate data and EEO-based traits, we account for both the immediate, direct effects of climate and the indirect, long-term effects that shape ecosystem PE. The combination of climatic factors and plant traits provides the highest explanatory power (coefficient of determination (R2), 0.80) and the lowest uncertainty (root mean squared error (RMSE), 30.5%) (Fig. 1c,f). These findings highlight the importance of an integrative approach to enhance our understanding of ecosystem PE. The influence of plant traits on PE persists across both weekly and biweekly timescales (Supplementary Fig. 13 and Supplementary Information). The robustness of these conclusions is further validated by analyses conducted exclusively on C4 vegetation, demonstrating an improvement in R2 from 54% to 84% compared with using climate data alone (Extended Data Fig. 2).
section: Results Plant traits and terrestrial ecosystem PE
title: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency

text: Having confirmed the critical role of plant traits in explaining ecosystem PE, we next identified specific traits that contribute additional explanatory power beyond climate variables. To achieve this, we assessed the independent contributions of RS-based traits (Chl, CIclump and LAI) and EEO-based traits (LL, LMA and Vcmax normalized at 25 °C (Vcmax25)) by evaluating how each trait improves model performance when added to a baseline model using only climate variables (Fig. 2). Integrating plant traits derived from either RS or EEO considerably enhances the model’s ability to explain the variance in ecosystem PE, while also reducing estimation errors across multiple metrics (Fig. 2). Among all the traits, LMA and LL were particularly impactful across R2, RMSE, slope and mean absolute percentage error metrics. However, Chl emerged as the most influential trait overall, as indicated by its Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) value, which reflects its additive contribution to the model’s predictions rather than the model’s quality compared with observations (Fig. 1e,f). The combined addition of all EEO traits outperformed the collective RS traits, and the integration of all plant traits (RS and EEO) delivered the best overall performance, underscoring the complementary strengths of these traits. These results highlight the efficacy of both RS and EEO methods in capturing the primary drivers of ecosystem PE, providing robust tools for tracking ecosystem productivity and detecting functional changes in response to climate change.

text: Conversely, to assess the additional contributions of climatic variables, we started with a baseline of plant traits only and subsequently incorporated climatic factors (Extended Data Fig. 3). Our findings confirm that while plant traits are the primary drivers of ecosystem PE, factors such as water availability and light conditions (CIcloud) also play crucial roles in mediating carbon fluxes (Fig. 1a,d and Extended Data Fig. 3). Specifically, although the evaporative stress index (ESI), defined as the ratio of actual to potential evapotranspiration, showed a moderate effect, only VPD and CIcloud notably improved the explanatory power (Extended Data Fig. 3). The limited enhancement from adding climate variables probably stems from the fact that EEO-derived plant traits have already partially incorporated climatic information through the EEO theory, such as the temperature-dependent maximum light-adapted quantum yield of photosystem II (Methods, equation (15)). These findings reinforce the necessity of an integrative approach that combines plant traits and climatology to fully understand ecosystem PE. The robustness of these conclusions is further supported by analyses using alternative datasets (for example, the MERIS Chl product; Extended Data Fig. 4).

text: To validate the robustness of our key findings from the general model, which was trained on the entire dataset (Figs. 1 and 2), we extended our analysis by training and evaluating the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) machine learning model separately for each plant functional type (PFT). This analysis was conducted under two scenarios: one considering only climatic factors, and the other incorporating both climatic factors and plant traits, with SHAP analysis providing further interpretive insights. Despite disparities in subset data sizes, the XGBoost model consistently performed relatively well in predicting ecosystem PE across global major PFTs (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Figs. 5 and 6). The model achieved a mean R2 ranging from 0.64 to 0.81 and RMSE from 22% to 49%, with slopes ranging from 0.85 to 1.03. Cropland exhibited the greatest improvement when plant trait information was incorporated (Fig. 3), followed by grassland, deciduous broadleaf forest and evergreen needleleaf forest. However, the limited data size for certain PFTs, such as savanna (validation n = 240), probably influenced model performance (Extended Data Fig. 6). text: To investigate how potential interaction effects shape the nonlinear contributions of plant traits to PE (Fig. 4), we analysed SHAP interaction values (Extended Data Fig. 7). While widespread coupling was observed among leaf traits, canopy structure and climate variables (Extended Data Fig. 7), our analysis focused on variables with Spearman’s ρ < 0.75 (Supplementary Fig. 2d). We selected this slightly higher threshold to balance reducing multicollinearity with the need to retain critical, closely related variables such as Chl, LAI and Vcmax25. Our findings uncover complex trade-offs among light distribution, harvesting efficiency and photosynthetic capacity, driven by interactions between canopy structure, biochemical traits and climate. For instance, elevated Chl amplifies the positive impact of CIcloud on PE, whereas lower CIcloud levels diminish this effect (Extended Data Figs. 4c and 8a). Notable interactions also emerge among LAI, Chl and Vcmax25, with dense canopies (LAI > 4) reducing the benefits of increased Chl on PE, probably due to light limitations (Extended Data Fig. 8b). This negative interaction is consistent across alternative Chl products (MERIS; Extended Data Fig. 4d). text: In this study, we present a data-driven framework that notably enhances our understanding of the key drivers behind ecosystem PE in the terrestrial biospheres (Figs. 1–4). Our analyses identify plant traits as valuable contributors to ecosystem PE across diverse global biomes and various timescales. Our findings reveal that the combination of plant traits and climate variables accounts for 80% (C3) to 84% (C4) of the variations in PE. This integrative approach provides new insights into the intricate interplay between biological and environmental factors that drive photosynthetic processes at the ecosystem level. Our findings highlight the critical role of plant traits in modulating ecosystem processes and indicate that relying solely on climatic variables or plant traits alone is inadequate to fully explain the intricate variations in these processes (Figs. 1 and 2). For instance, previous studies have shown that the effect of VPD on ecosystem PE varies across biomes39,40. This complexity may be due to its interaction with temperature10,41 or decoupling from soil moisture42,43, or potentially unaccounted-for plant traits. Moreover, our results show that climatic variables influence photosynthesis indirectly through interactions with leaf traits. For instance, an increase in diffuse radiation enhances light availability on shaded leaves44, which, when paired with high Chl, leads to more efficient light use, thereby boosting canopy photosynthesis45–48. This interaction between diffuse radiation and Chl vividly illustrates the necessity of considering both climatic factors and plant traits in tandem in ecosystem modelling. Canopy structure is crucial for unravelling the complexities of ecosystem photosynthesis49,50. Canopy structure influences the light environment via radiative transfer, directly affecting light absorption and photosynthetic activity30. In dense canopies with high LAI, light penetration is notably reduced, particularly in the lower canopy layers, as described by the Beer–Lambert law51. This leads to light-limited photosynthesis in shaded leaves, diminishing the overall contribution of chlorophyll pigments (Extended Data Fig. 8b). The interplay between diffuse radiation and chlorophyll (Extended Data Figs. 4c and 8a) highlights a critical point: while plants have evolved to optimize light capture through vertical gradients in leaf nitrogen and chlorophyll52,53, our findings raise questions about how these gradients interact with diffuse light. Future studies incorporating multi-layer canopy modelling and higher-resolution data are needed to explore whether these gradients represent the most effective strategy under varying light regimes.

text: processes54,55. Chl is commonly used to empirically parameterize Vcmax25 (ref. 56), though future work could explore its direct integration by modifying parameters related to light absorption and energy conversion (for example, Jmax), especially under fluctuating light conditions. LL can also constrain Vcmax25 as a function of relative age to indicate the leaf turnover rate, although this remains an empirical approach57. Similarly, LMA could be explored as a constraint on other traits, such as LAI and Vcmax25, given its role within a broader network of interconnected plant traits that collectively govern plant performance58,59. To refine photosynthesis models, evaluations should focus on PE rather than solely on GPP, which is often dominated by canopy structure. Therefore, while it is crucial to incorporate key plant traits into dynamic global vegetation models to better capture phenomena such as extreme climate events and interannual GPP variations, this effort must carefully balance simplicity, realism and uncertainty6,60. However, these efforts are hindered by the limited availability of global plant trait data. We propose an interdisciplinary approach that leverages climate data, RS (for example, Chl, LAI and CIclump)61,62, EEO principles (for example, LL, LMA and Vcmax25)26,63 and global plant trait databases22,64. This integration is essential for a comprehensive understanding of how ecosystem-scale photosynthesis responds to environmental changes. Leaf nitrogen and phosphorus are critical yet underrepresented traits for understanding ecosystem PE, primarily due to the scarcity of continuous, broad-scale data65. By integrating empirically derived leaf nitrogen and phosphorus content into our models, we notably improved their explanatory power and overall performance (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Information). This enhancement underscores the critical role these nutrients play in regulating ecosystem productivity66,67. However, the strong correlations between nitrogen, phosphorus and Vcmax25 suggest potential confounding effects, making the interpretation challenging.

section: Discussion
title: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency

text: While EEO models offer valuable insights into capturing the spatial variation among sites in traits such as LL and LMA26, they rely on the assumption of a steady state relative to long-term (for example, growing season) environmental conditions. This reliance makes it challenging to predict seasonal dynamics accurately. However, this limitation does not extend to Vcmax25 (ref. 63). Additionally, EEO methods are predominantly driven by climate, making them less direct than approaches that consider light absorption features linked to leaf chemical composition. Hyperspectral RS has shown notable promise in mapping global plant traits, with current operational missions (for example, EnMAP and GF-5) and upcoming missions (for example, SBG and CHIME)70 offering enhanced spatial–temporal resolution and accuracy, particularly for traits such as Chl, leaf nitrogen and LMA. Moreover, the integration of solar-induced fluorescence measurements has emerged as a powerful tool to directly assess plant photosynthetic activity, providing complementary insights into vegetation function71. These advancements could greatly improve our ability to capture the spatial–temporal patterns of vegetation characteristics, including PE, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of ecosystem responses to climate change. However, accurately incorporating plant traits and representing photosynthesis in Earth system models—whether through empirical or mechanistic approaches—remains a notable challenge and a crucial objective for future research6,60,72,73. A hybrid modelling approach that integrates process-based models with the adaptability of data-driven machine learning offers a promising path forward74.

section: Discussion
title: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency

text: We used the FLUXNET2015 Tier 1 daily dataset, which covers the eddy covariance flux measurements of carbon, water vapour and energy exchange between ecosystems and the atmosphere75. We used daily GPP data (GPP_NT_VUT_REF) based on the nighttime decomposition method76. Daily gap-filled meteorological records include air temperature (TA_F), incoming surface shortwave radiation (SW_IN_F), potential shortwave radiation (SW_IN_POT), surface pressure (PA_F), VPD (VPD_F), CO2 (CO2_F_MDS) and shallow SWC (SWC_F_MDS_1). All data were filtered using a data quality control threshold set at >0.8. We also excluded negative GPP, VPD, SWC and CO2 data. We calculated CIcloud as the alternative for the fraction of diffuse solar radiation9: SWINF CIcloud = 1 −( (1) ) SWINPOT where SWINF is incoming surface shortwave radiation and SWINPOT is potential shortwave radiation. Ecosystem PE is defined as GPP normalized by APAR: GPP PE = (2) fPAR × PPFD where fPAR (unitless) is the fraction of APAR (mol photons per m2 per day) obtained from MODIS MOD15A2H (eight-day, 18 February 2000 to 3 July 2002) and MCD15A3H (four-day, 4 July 2002 onwards) v.6.1 929 products, both at a 1.0 × 1.0 km2 resolution. The original data were quality controlled (FparLai_QC and FparExtra_QC) and smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter. fPAR was interpolated to daily scale using the Akima interpolator for gaps smaller than 50%77. Moreover, to assess uncertainties stemming from the choice of fPAR products, we compared results with additional quality-controlled 1-km GEOV2 fPAR (ten-day, 1 January 2000 onwards)78 (Supplementary Fig. 12). PPFD (mol photons per m2 per day) is the photosynthetic photon flux density estimated as a function of SW_IN_F (W m−2) using a multiplier of 2.04 μmol J−1 (ref. 79). We calculated PE at three temporal scales: daily, 7-day mean and 14-day mean, using consecutive gap-free and non-overlapping rolling windows accordingly to prevent temporal autocorrelation (Supplementary Fig. 13b,c). PE was further constrained to values greater than 0.001 mol C per mol photons and less than 0.12 mol C per mol photons9.

text: Our final dataset included 120 sites and 10 PFTs defined by the IGBP (Supplementary Table 1), including 6 EBF sites, 16 DBF sites, 7 MF sites, 28 ENF sites, 6 WSA sites, 6 SAV sites, 2 CSH sites, 8 OSH sites, 27 GRA sites and 14 CRO sites. Wetlands were excluded from this study, and C4 sites (Supplementary Table 1) were analysed separately (Extended Data Fig. 2). All data were constrained to the growing season using a consistent temperature threshold set at >10 °C (5 °C was also tested; Supplementary Fig. 13a), considering CRO inclusion.

text: We applied EEO theory to simulate site-specific LMA, LL and Vcmax25 (normalized to 25 °C)26,63,80. EEO theory hypothesizes that the relationship between LMA and LL will maximize leaf net carbon gain26. Hence, the community site-mean LMA for deciduous (LMAde: CRO, GRA, DBF and SAV) and evergreen (LMAev: ENF and EBF) taxa can be estimated by these equations, with detailed derivations available in previous studies26,68: ln (LMAde) = ln ( f ) + ln (Iabs) −0.052Ta + βα,deαbess + β0,de (3) ln (LMAev) = 0.25 ln ( f ) + 0.5 ln (Iabs) −0.013Ta + βα,evαbess + β0,ev (4) where f is the fraction of growing season (defined as the period with daily mean temperature >10 °C) length to a year; Iabs (mol photons per m2 per day) is the mean growing season canopy APAR; Ta (K) is the mean growing season air temperature; βα,ev, βα,de, β0,ev and β0,de are empirical coefficients derived from Glopnet22 and China Plant Trait Database64 (Supplementary Table 2); and αbess is an ESI computed as the ratio of actual to potential evapotranspiration (ET/PET) simulated using the process model Breathing Earth System Simulator (BESS v.2.0)54. Due to limitations in trait data, direct validation of LMA across FLUXNET2015 sites is still challenging; however, validation of EEO-derived LMA against global plant trait databases shows good performance68.

text: We used a recently released global eight-day Chl product at 500-m resolution covering the period from 2000 to 202062. The Chl data were produced from MODIS surface reflectance, where the effects of LAI and canopy non-photosynthetic material were excluded using radiative transfer models. The Chl data have shown good agreement with ground measurements and reasonable seasonal variations in different PFTs62. To align the Chl data with the footprints of FLUXNET2015 sites, we extracted nine pixels, including eight adjacent to the site pixel, and computed their mean as the community site value (1.5 × 1.5 km2). The eight-day Chl data were further interpolated to a daily scale using the Akima method for gaps smaller than 50%. Moreover, to assess uncertainties stemming from the choice of Chl products, we compared the results with an additional seven-day MERIS Chl product at 300-m resolution spanning from 2003 to 2012 (ref. 61) (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. 10). We processed the MERIS Chl data to a daily scale using the Akima method77 and resampled them to a 900-m resolution.

text: LAI data were obtained from MODIS MOD15A2H (eight-day, 18 February 2000 to 3 July 2002) and MCD15A3H (four-day, 4 July 2002 onwards) v.6.1 products, both at a 1.0 × 1.0 km2 resolution. The original data were quality controlled (FparLai_QC and FparExtra_QC) and smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter. The LAI data were further interpolated to a daily scale using the Akima interpolator for gaps smaller than 50%77. Similarly, CIclump data at the site level were obtained from a global 500-m product derived from MODIS BRDF data87. We applied the same method as MODIS LAI to derive daily CIclump. Moreover, to assess uncertainties stemming from the choice of LAI products, we compared the results with additional GLASS LAI products at a daily and 1.0 × 1.0 km2 resolution88 (Supplementary Fig. 11).
section: Canopy structure
title: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency

text: We deployed three candidate machine learning models, including deep neural networks, light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM) and XGBoost, to associate leaf traits (Chl, LL, Vcmax25 and LMA), canopy structure (LAI and CIclump) and meteorological variables (CIcloud, Ta, SWC, VPD, ESI and CO2) with ecosystem PE. CO2 was included to assess potential fertilization effects. The complete information for all explanatory variables is provided in Supplementary Section 1.2. To prevent collinearity and redundancy among input variables, we performed a variance inflation factor (VIF) analysis, setting a threshold of VIF < 10 (Supplementary Table 3), and a non-parametric Spearman correlation analysis with a threshold of ρ < 0.75 (Supplementary Fig. 2d). Detailed information about the structure and parameters for each model is shown in our publicly available code. Starting with the default hyperparameter values (for example, for XGBoost, n_estimators, 100; max_depth, 6; and learning_rate, 0.3), we tuned one parameter at a time until further adjustments no longer resulted in notable improvements in model performance. We developed the deep neural network model using a systematic approach, starting with a shallow network of three hidden layers and gradually increasing the depth on the basis of performance. Neuron counts were selected as follows: 128, 128, 64, 64, 32, 32, 16, 16, 8 and 8 to balance model complexity and computational efficiency, with reduced neuron counts in deeper layers to minimize overfitting. ReLU activation was used in the hidden layers, as it outperformed the Tanh function, effectively addressing the vanishing gradient problem. To ensure reliable estimates of model performance, we implemented a k-fold cross-validation scheme with k set to either five or ten. In each iteration, 80% (for k = 5) or 90% (for k = 10) of the data were used for training, while the remaining 20% or 10% were used for validation. The evaluation matrix includes R2, RMSE, the slope of the regression line and the bias of estimation.

title: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency

text: On the basis of the final averaged matrix (Supplementary Fig. 5), we selected XGBoost to further investigate the underlying mechanisms governing ecosystem-scale PE (‘Mechanistic interpretation of machine learning models’). Although LightGBM produced comparable performance, XGBoost was preferred due to its robust handling of small to medium-sized datasets, finer control over regularization and proven success in similar ecological studies42,89,90.
section: Developing and screening machine learning models
title: Plant traits shape global spatiotemporal variations in photosynthetic efficiency

text: To quantify and interpret the contributions, potential nonlinearity and interactions among leaf traits, canopy structure and climate on ecosystem PE, we integrated cooperative game theory principles (SHAP values) into the black-box machine learning models. Cooperative game theory deals with situations where groups of players cooperate to achieve a common goal, often by forming coalitions91. In this context, each feature (for example, Chl) in a machine learning model can be seen as a player, and the goal is to cooperate with other variables to estimate ecosystem PE accurately. Here we used the SHAP TreeExplainer to compute SHAP values for decision-tree-based models (XGBoost and LightGBM) and KernelExplainer for the deep neural network model91,92. SHAP is a state-of-the-art model-agnostic method that not only offers local explanations but also interprets the global model structure on the basis of numerous local explanations. SHAP values provide a fair attribution of importance by considering all possible combinations of input variables, ensuring that each trait’s influence is evaluated in the context of others. This approach therefore enables us to unveil the primary effects (SHAP values) of each feature as well as potential interactive effects (SHAP interaction values) in a theoretically grounded way91. XGBoost and SHAP methods have been successfully applied in multidisciplinary studies42,89,90.
